questions.q: Why must the impossible-travel rule group events by user_id instead of evaluating each login independently?
options: A single login can never be impossible on its own - it's only impossible compared to another login from the same identity
Grouping by user_id makes the rule run faster, with no effect on accuracy
SIEM correlation rules are legally required to group by account
Individual logins are never logged by the SIEM, only grouped ones
questions.explain: Impossible travel is a comparison between two events from the same account, which requires grouping by identity first.

questions.q: What does the rule's 60-minute correlation window actually do?
options: Forces the analyst to review the alert within 60 minutes or it auto-closes
Deletes any login events older than 60 minutes from the SIEM
Bounds how far apart in time two logins can be and still be compared as potentially related
Sets the maximum number of alerts the rule can generate per hour
questions.explain: The window is generous enough to catch Lesson 29's 39-minute gap without comparing logins that are unrelated days apart.

questions.q: Why does the rule calculate a required travel speed instead of matching against a list of suspicious countries?
options: A speed calculation is durable against any two distant locations, including ones never previously flagged, while a fixed list ages badly and misses plenty
Speed calculations are required by every major SIEM vendor
Country lists are more accurate than speed calculations in every case
It removes the need for any correlation window at all
questions.explain: Calculating required speed generalizes to any location pair, unlike a hardcoded list that only catches countries someone already thought to flag.

questions.q: Why would this rule, unfixed, generate false positives against Thornfield's own corporate VPN?
options: VPN traffic is never logged by the SIEM, so the rule can't see it at all
Corporate VPNs always disable MFA, which the rule treats as inherently suspicious
The rule only evaluates traffic from countries outside North America
A VPN exit node can appear in a different country than the employee's real location, mimicking impossible travel
questions.explain: VPN routing can make a login appear to originate somewhere other than the user's actual location, creating a false geographic jump.

questions.q: What is the correct tuning fix for the VPN exit-node problem described in Step 4?
options: Ignore the issue, since VPN-related false positives are rare enough to not matter
Add a known exit-node exception that lowers severity rather than suppressing the alert entirely
Block all VPN traffic from leaving the country of origin
Disable the entire impossible-travel rule whenever VPN traffic is present
questions.explain: Lowering severity for known exit-node ranges keeps the alert reviewable instead of either flooding the queue or hiding it completely.
